1: Module context: The Direction module (Strategy Intent & Direction Across Functions) equips participants to understand how each Executive Leadership role interprets strategic intent and direction, and the steps where these interpretations create cross-functional tension or reinforcement.
Participants work through the whole Direction module from the perspective of their assigned CXO role.
4: Preamble (further wording): Leaders agree on what strategy means in the precise, strategic sense, translated to operational reality, that makes every subsequent decision coherent.

This unit opens with the master definition of strategy, unpacks each of its critical components, and builds toward two integrated outputs: a Strategic Intent Statement and a Success in Practice narrative.
6: Why a master definition: Strategy is frequently used but rarely precisely defined. In most organisations it functions as shorthand for ambition, planning, or competitive intention, with each executive leader carrying a slightly different version of the word. In the Strategy2Results® framework, strategy has a specific applied definition.
How the definition is unpacked: for each critical concept, what it means, what it implies for execution, and what breaks when it is absent.
7: OUTPUT: The decided position is distinct from a plan, a meeting, the process of strategising, the presentation deck, and the off-site discussion.
ITERATIVE: This rules out strategy as an annual ritual and rules in strategy as a living organisational capability.
THINKING & LOGIC: Strategy needs reasoning as well as inspiration.
PROCESS: With process, strategy stops being a personality-dependent event. Process is the scaffolding that makes thinking transferable.
WHAT · WHY · HOW · WHEN: Together the four dimensions constitute a complete strategic position. A third failure pattern: WHEN without WHAT is urgency without direction.
CREATES · DELIVERS · SUSTAINS: The failure mode is named “partial value chains”.
STAKEHOLDERS: The blind spots are specific: employees who deliver value, investors who fund it, regulators who permit it.
8: What strategic intent is: Strategic intent is the crystallisation of the 3Ws and H into a single, expressible position. It is the directional anchor from which every other strategic choice must flow, and it stops short of being the full strategy. The four dimensions are interdependent: answering only two or three creates a structurally incomplete strategy.
Critical Insight (further detail): Unclear WHAT and WHY are seldom the cause of failure. For HOW, high-level aspiration is insufficient. For WHEN, a project milestone list is insufficient.
Further core questions. WHY: Why does our approach create more value than others? HOW: How do we organise and resource the work?
WHEN, the pace question in full: Are we moving at the right pace, fast enough to catch the windows and slow enough to build solidly?
A well-formed strategic intent answers all four questions simultaneously:
WHAT: What value are we creating?
WHY: Why will stakeholders choose us?
HOW: How will we deliver this value?

Without a clear strategic intent (further consequences): Every investment becomes a negotiation without a shared reference point. Every performance review becomes a contest between competing definitions of success. Strategic intent is not a slogan.
9: From intent to future reality: Once the strategic intent is locked (once the organisation has answered WHAT, WHY, HOW, and WHEN), the next step is to translate that cognitive clarity into an observable future reality. The facilitator guides the team through a deliberate shift.
Further line for the facilitation move: “Assume the strategy has worked. From here, we are observing.” Intentions and plans stay out of the description.

The 3W1H in lived form, in the order listed above: WHAT (the value as customers experience it), WHY (stakeholder trust, choice and advocacy), HOW (the way the organisation operates), WHEN (pace, sequencing and responsiveness).
Why four domains: Anchoring the narrative in four observable domains that determine success in practice avoids vague storytelling.

What SiP does: Success in Practice (SiP) translates strategic intent into a clear picture of the future operating reality of the organisation. It answers the question that most strategy processes fail to address clearly (the question quoted above).
This framing produces several critical effects for an executive team:
- Removes ambiguity about what the strategy is actually aiming to produce.
- Creates a shared mental model of the future state across all functions.
- Provides a decision filter: every initiative, investment, and priority can be tested against it.
- Enables recognition of progress: leaders can see alignment and momentum during execution.
The two forms of SiP (further detail):

Headline: The short-form expression of the SiP. Memorable, inspirational, and directional. It is the portable version of the strategy, repeated in operational reviews as well as in meetings, town halls and board discussions.

Storyline: It enables leaders to visualise the future organisation as if it already exists. The leadership conversation moves from debating abstract strategic ideas to describing an operating reality.
12: Why co-creation is a requirement: Strategy execution fails when leaders interpret the strategy through different perspectives, pursue different definitions of success, or prioritise different outcomes.
What co-creation excludes: a Strategic Intent Statement and SiP written by one executive and distributed to the rest of the organisation, and agreement on the destination reached through compliance.
The third result in full: the organisation builds collective ownership of the future state.
13: Why three components: Strategy is not produced in a single session.
Thinking Logic: Reaching strategic insight takes judgement as well as analysis. Strategic errors arise in logic far more often than in data.

Process: The scaffolding takes the form of workshops, governance forums, and decision protocols. The five stages in full: Diagnose (understand reality without filtering); Interpret (extract meaning); Design (formulate choices and trade-offs); Validate (stress-test assumptions); Refine (loop back and improve). When process is over-engineered, strategy becomes template-filling.
Where most organisations fail (the full result): strategy that is internally coherent but fundamentally incorrect, and confidence that is not grounded in sound logic.
14: Strategic Alignment (further detail): Strategic Intent guards against each executive pursuing a personal interpretation of the domain and its differentiating logic. SiP guards against each executive describing a functional version of the future operating state.
15: Section opening: The SiP dimensions serve as a guardrail that carries the intent into future success. No dimension is a single metric. This section breaks each dimension down into its key indicators.
16: CARE source encounters: Customers encounter the organisation through four channels, and each one is the source of one form of value. People: Connection Value. Platforms: Access Value. Products: Results Value. Processes: Effort Value.
D1 · Connection Value: Customers trust that the care extends beyond the transaction. When it is missing, customers feel processed where they should feel served.
D1 · Effort Value: The minimal effort is the customer’s own effort to achieve results. No complexity is passed to the customer.
D2 · Decision Flow: The organisation does not bottleneck at the top. When it is missing, it is the leaders below CXO level who feel they cannot act without approval.
D2 · Cross-Functional Coordination: Execution friction that is silently absorbed goes unmanaged.

D2 · Delivery Rhythm: The cadence is weekly signal scanning, monthly performance reads, and quarterly strategic review. When it is missing, review has not become a disciplined organisational habit, and delivery is variable and unpredictable.
D3 · Cross-Boundary Collaboration: Information is shared proactively. When it is missing, information is hoarded or filtered.
D3 · Ownership Culture: People step in without being required to. Accountability is cultural before it is structural. When it is missing and something fails at a boundary, no one steps forward.
D3 · Strategic Alignment: Leaders can trace what they are doing to both the strategic intent and the SiP. When it is missing, function history is one of the things driving action.

D3 · Dialogue Quality: Leaders can say they do not know something without losing credibility. When it is missing, System 1 thinking (fast, pattern-based) dominates without System 2 (deliberate, analytical) to check it.
D4 · Growth Trajectory: Growth is deliberate. When it is missing, growth may be happening in arenas that were not part of the intended WHAT.
D4 · Profitability Quality: The premium is earned because the organisation has chosen arenas where its differentiation commands it.
D4 · Market Position: The stakeholders in question are customers, partners, analysts and employees. When it is missing, the strategy exists on paper only.
D4 · Value Durability: The organisation is building moats. When it is missing, short-term results also cost the relationships that make future success possible.
18: Anchor question: How do all executive perspectives integrate into one Strategic Intent Statement and one shared SiP?
20: Diagnostic questions (open-response version): The assessment covers all 26 components of the master strategy definition. For each area, the executive team records its honest diagnostic response in a Team Response column, then scores the area 0–3.
A · Process
1. OUTPUT: Can your strategy be expressed in a single written statement that someone not in the room could act on? Describe what exists today.
2. ITERATIVE: Describe the last time your strategy was formally updated in response to new information. What changed, and what triggered the revision?
3. THINKING & LOGIC: What uncomfortable assumption does your current strategy rest on that has not been formally challenged? What would happen if that assumption were wrong?
4. PROCESS: Describe your current strategy process. Who is involved? What decisions are made? Could someone else run the next cycle without you?
B · Intent (3W1H)
5. WHAT: State your WHAT in one precise sentence, including what you have explicitly decided NOT to do. Where does your scope end?
6. WHY: What is the unique reason stakeholders choose your organisation over every alternative, including doing nothing? Could a competitor make the same claim?
7. HOW: What are the two or three specific capabilities that make your strategy executable? Where are the most critical capability gaps right now?
8. WHEN: What is the sequencing logic of your current strategy? What must happen first, and why does that order matter?
C · Value
9. CREATES value: What new value are you currently generating that did not exist before? How do you know it is genuinely valued by its intended recipients?
10. DELIVERS value: How reliably does your created value reach the people it was designed for? Where in the delivery system is the biggest breakdown?
11. SUSTAINS value: What are you explicitly investing in today that ensures your strategy will still be relevant in three to five years, well beyond next quarter?
D · Environment
12. STAKEHOLDERS: Name all the stakeholder groups your strategy must serve. Which group are you most likely underserving right now, and what risk does that create?
13. NAVIGATING (continuous course correction, beyond reacting or surviving): Describe the most deliberate move your organisation has made in the last 12 months to shape its environment.
14. THE FORCES: Which force in your operating environment poses the greatest threat to your strategy in the next 18 months, and how explicitly does your strategy address it?
15. OPERATING ENVIRONMENT: How recently has your operating environment been formally scanned? What is the most significant environmental shift you are currently under-responding to?
E · Engine
Areas 16 to 18 have no open-response question in this set; use the scoring questions listed above.
F · Strategic Chain
19. INPUTS: How complete, current, and unbiased are your strategic inputs right now? What critical input is most likely missing?
20. ITERATIVE THINKING LOGIC (mental model and reasoning): Where in your strategy work is thinking most rigorous? Where is it most likely to drift into assumption-confirming analysis?

21. STRUCTURED PROCESS CYCLES (formalised iteration that turns thinking into documented positions): How structured and consistent is your strategy process? Could someone step in and run the next cycle without the current lead person?
22. DECISIONS ACROSS WHAT / WHY / HOW / WHEN: Which of the four dimensions (WHAT, WHY, HOW, or WHEN) is least clearly documented in your current strategy?
23. VALUE LIFECYCLE DESIGN: Which stage of your value lifecycle is weakest (creating, delivering, or sustaining), and what evidence tells you that?
24. STAKEHOLDER ALIGNMENT (multi-constituency logic): Which stakeholder group creates the greatest risk if their expectations are consistently not met, and how explicit is your strategy’s response?

25. ENVIRONMENTAL NAVIGATION (external and internal forces): What internal force (culture, legacy, habits, or inertia) is most likely to undermine your strategy, and how explicitly are you addressing it?

26. OUTPUT (a set of choices that answers all four dimensions): Could your complete strategy be communicated clearly by someone who was not in the room? Write it as a test: what would a one-page version say?
24: How the results are used: The executive team conducts the assessment using the 26 areas of strategy as defined by the programme. The corrective actions across the four SiP dimensions enhance the intent, and the team then crafts the SiP storyline and headline.
26: The table layout: one row per CXO role (CEO, CFO, COO, CHRO, CTO, CMO, CCO, CPO, CRO, CSO) and one column per SiP dimension (Customer Experience & Value; Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm; People & Culture Dynamics; Enterprise Value Creation). Each CXO uses the maturity assessment results to describe the four dimensions.
31: The two outputs: This unit produces two integrated outputs from one collective exercise.
- A Strategic Intent Statement: a precise articulation of WHAT the organisation does, for WHOM, WHY it is distinctively positioned, and what it deliberately excludes.
- A Success in Practice (SiP) Narrative: a vivid, four-dimensional description of the organisation written in the present tense of the future, co-owned by the entire executive team.
Further detail for each stage of the summary:
Awareness: Each concept in the master definition carries a specific strategic implication as well as a named failure mode. The Storyline is written in the present tense of the future.
Intelligence: When executives participate in shaping both outputs, strategy moves from individual interpretation to shared strategic imagination.

Extrapolating: Strategic intent most often breaks down at the point of execution across functions, where each area interprets the strategy differently. To make this fragmentation visible, the SiP dimensions act as diagnostics, translating strategy into observable signals across four critical domains. Leaders assess whether the strategy is working by examining how customers experience value, how the organisation operates and executes, how people behave and align, and whether enterprise value is being created and sustained. Each dimension reveals specific indicators of alignment or breakdown, enabling leaders to identify execution gaps, surface hidden friction, and locate the precise points where strategy is not translating into reality.

Integration: The six groups of the assessment are Process Components (OUTPUT, ITERATIVE, THINKING & LOGIC, PROCESS); Strategic Intent Dimensions (WHAT, WHY, HOW, WHEN); Value Lifecycle (CREATES, DELIVERS, SUSTAINS); Operating Environment (STAKEHOLDERS, NAVIGATING, THE FORCES, OPERATING ENVIRONMENT); Strategy Engine (Thinking Logic, Process, Iterative Nature); and Strategic Chain (Inputs through Coherent Output). The results were used to identify corrective actions across the four SiP dimensions and to anchor the storyline and headline.
By the end of the session, the executive team has produced:
- A collectively authored Success in Practice storyline.
- A shared mental model of the future organisation.
